learn.title: Direct Air Capture: Removing CO2 with Renewables
learn.intro: Direct Air Capture (DAC) pulls CO2 straight from ambient air using renewable energy, offering a critical tool to offset hard-to-abate emissions. As global temperatures rise, DAC provides a scalable solution to reduce atmospheric CO2, especially when paired with clean power sources like solar and wind. It’s a key technology in achieving net-zero goals by 2050.
learn.c1_text: India emits over 2.7 billion tons of CO2 annually, making it the third-largest emitter globally. Integrating DAC into India’s renewable expansion could help meet its net-zero by 2070 commitment. Pilot projects are being explored in Gujarat and Rajasthan, leveraging abundant solar resources for carbon removal.
learn.c2_text: DAC requires significant energy—about 300–500 kWh per ton of CO2 captured. Pairing DAC with solar or wind ensures low-cost, clean power. Excess renewable energy during peak production can be diverted to DAC plants instead of going to waste. This synergy helps stabilize grids while actively reducing atmospheric CO2 levels.

learn.stat2: Global DAC capacity reached 40 million tons in 2022
learn.stat3: DAC uses 300–500 kWh of electricity per ton of CO2 captured
learn.stat4: India emits approximately 2.7 billion tons of CO2 per year

learn.title: Floating Offshore Wind: Deep Water Power
learn.intro: Floating offshore wind unlocks vast wind resources in deep waters where traditional turbines cannot operate. These platforms enable countries to access stronger, more consistent winds far from shore, dramatically expanding renewable energy potential. As nations push for clean energy, floating wind offers a path to large-scale offshore deployment beyond coastal limits.
learn.c1_text: Fixed-bottom turbines require shallow waters (less than 60 meters deep), limiting where they can be installed. Floating turbines are moored to the seabed with cables and anchors, allowing operation in depths over 600 meters. Imagine a boat anchored in open ocean—this design opens up 80% of offshore wind potential previously unreachable.
learn.c2_text: Floating wind turbines sit on buoyant platforms stabilized by mooring lines and dynamic positioning. They can be spar-type, semi-submersible, or tension-leg platforms. Each design balances stability and cost. The rotor blades spin as usual, generating electricity transmitted via underwater cables to onshore grids.
learn.c3_text: India has identified 370 GW of offshore wind potential, much of it in deep waters off Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. The National Offshore Wind Energy Corporation (NOWERC) plans demonstration projects. Floating wind could play a major role in meeting India’s 500 GW non-fossil target by 2030.
learn.stat1: India has 370 GW of identified offshore wind potential
learn.stat2: Floating wind can operate in water depths greater than 600 meters
learn.stat3: Over 80% of global offshore wind potential lies in deep waters suitable for floating platforms
learn.stat4: India plans to commission 30 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2030

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels: Power from Both Sides
learn.intro: Bifacial solar panels generate electricity from both their front and back sides, capturing reflected sunlight and increasing energy yield. Unlike traditional monofacial panels, they harness albedo—the amount of light reflected from surfaces like snow, sand, or white roofs. This innovation boosts efficiency and lowers the cost per watt of solar installations.
learn.c1_text: Bifacial panels have solar cells on both sides, often encased in transparent backsheets or glass-glass modules. When sunlight hits the panel, electrons move and create current. Reflected light from the ground also hits the rear side, generating extra power. On average, bifacial panels produce 10–20% more energy than standard ones.
learn.c2_text: Albedo refers to how much light a surface reflects. Fresh snow has an albedo of 80%, while asphalt is around 5%. Installing bifacial panels over reflective surfaces like white membranes or gravel increases output. For example, a farm in Arizona saw 27% higher yield using bifacial panels compared to conventional ones.
learn.c3_text: India’s National Solar Mission promotes advanced PV technologies. Several large-scale projects now use bifacial modules. In Rajasthan’s Jodhpur airport project, bifacial panels were installed to maximize land use. With high solar irradiance and clear skies, India is ideal for deploying these high-efficiency panels.

learn.stat2: Bifacial panels increase energy yield by 10–20% on average
learn.stat3: Snow-covered ground reflects up to 80% of sunlight (albedo value)

learn.title: Tidal Stream Energy: Ocean Currents as Power
learn.intro: Tidal stream energy converts the kinetic force of moving water into electricity using underwater turbines. Unlike unpredictable wind or solar, tides follow precise lunar cycles, making this one of the most predictable renewable sources. Countries with strong coastal currents are investing in tidal tech to diversify their clean energy mix.
learn.c1_text: Underwater turbines resemble underwater windmills, placed in fast-moving tidal streams. As tides flow, blades rotate to drive generators. A single device can produce continuous power for decades. For instance, Scotland’s MeyGen project generates enough electricity for 2,000 homes using just four turbines in the Pentland Firth.
learn.c2_text: Tides are driven by gravitational pulls from the moon and sun, making them highly predictable decades ahead. This reliability allows utilities to plan generation schedules accurately. Tidal energy also has minimal visual impact and low environmental disruption when sited properly, making it ideal for coastal regions.
learn.c3_text: India’s coastline stretches over 7,500 km, with strong tidal activity in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is studying tidal potential in Gujarat and Kerala. Pilot projects could soon tap into India’s estimated 1 GW of exploitable tidal energy.
learn.stat1: India has a coastline of over 7,500 km
learn.stat2: MeyGen project in Scotland powers 2,000 homes with four turbines
learn.stat3: Tidal energy is predictable up to 100% accuracy decades in advance

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements: Financing Renewables
learn.intro: A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) is a long-term contract between an energy buyer and seller, locking in prices and securing financing for renewable projects. PPAs provide revenue certainty for developers and stable rates for buyers. They’ve become the backbone of corporate renewable procurement, enabling companies to source clean energy at competitive costs.
learn.c1_text: In a PPA, a developer builds a solar or wind farm and sells electricity to a utility or corporation over 15–25 years. The buyer agrees to purchase power at a fixed rate, often lower than market prices. This guarantees returns for investors, reducing financial risk and unlocking capital needed to build new renewable capacity.
learn.c2_text: Large corporations like Google and Amazon sign virtual PPAs to meet sustainability goals. These deals don’t involve physical delivery—they’re financial contracts settled based on market differences. By 2023, corporations had signed over 7 GW of renewable PPAs globally, driving demand for new wind and solar farms.
learn.c3_text: Indian companies like Tata Motors and Infosys have signed PPAs to source green power. The government supports open access policies, allowing industries to buy direct from renewable generators. With falling tariffs, PPAs offer attractive pricing—solar tariffs dropped below ₹2/kWh in recent auctions.
learn.stat1: Corporate PPAs reached 7.2 GW globally in 2023
learn.stat2: India's solar tariff fell below ₹2 per kWh in recent auctions
learn.stat3: PPAs typically span 15–25 years for revenue stability
learn.stat4: Over 7 GW of corporate renewable PPAs signed globally in 2023

learn.title: Floating Solar Farms: Water-Based Clean Energy
learn.intro: Floating solar farms install photovoltaic panels on bodies of water like reservoirs, lakes, and ponds. This approach saves land, reduces evaporation, and improves panel performance due to cooling effects. It’s especially valuable in densely populated or land-scarce regions seeking to expand solar capacity without competing for space.
learn.c1_text: Floating solar arrays reduce water evaporation by up to 30%, preserving freshwater in drought-prone areas. Panels also run cooler on water, boosting efficiency by 5–10%. Anchored pontoons keep them stable, while underwater cables connect to nearby substations. China leads with over 100 floating solar projects.
learn.c2_text: Corrosion resistance and anchoring systems are key concerns. Specialized coatings protect metal parts, while flexible mooring lines adapt to water level changes. Maintenance requires boats or amphibious vehicles. Despite higher upfront costs, LCOE is declining as technology matures and economies of scale emerge.
learn.c3_text: India has launched 45 floating solar projects across states like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Madhya Pradesh. The 150 MW Ramagundam project in Telangana is among the largest. NITI Aayog targets 10 GW of floating solar by 2030, leveraging India’s 420 sq km of suitable water bodies for deployment.
learn.stat1: India plans 10 GW of floating solar capacity by 2030
learn.stat2: Floating solar reduces water evaporation by up to 30%
learn.stat3: Panel efficiency increases by 5–10% due to cooling on water
learn.stat4: China operates over 100 floating solar installations
